name: Evening primrose oil

card.summary: A gamma-linolenic acid-rich seed oil sold as a supplement and skin product; reviews find insufficient evidence for eczema or other conditions.
card.note: May increase bleeding risk; caution advised in pregnancy and seizure disorders.

quick.overview:
Evening primrose oil is pressed from the seeds of Oenothera biennis, a North American plant. It contains linoleic acid and gamma-linolenic acid (GLA) and is sold mainly as an oral dietary supplement, also appearing in skin-care products.

It has been studied for atopic eczema, breast pain, menopausal symptoms and other conditions. The US National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health, as summarised in reference sources, describes the evidence as insufficient for any medical condition, and a Cochrane review found no effect on eczema.
quick.mechanism: GLA is an omega-6 fatty acid that the body converts to prostaglandin precursors; proponents argue this supports skin barrier and inflammatory balance. The proposed link to appearance outcomes has mostly been tested in eczema rather than cosmetic skin quality.
quick.risks: Described as likely safe at recommended amounts, with headache and nausea reported. It may raise bleeding risk, and sources advise caution in people with seizure disorders or mania and in pregnancy or breastfeeding. Herb-drug interaction reviews list it among herbal products of interest.

lead: Evening primrose oil (EPO) is a vegetable oil obtained from the seeds of the common evening primrose, Oenothera biennis, a North American plant that became naturalised across much of the world.[1] The seeds contain about 24 percent oil, rich in the polyunsaturated fatty acids linoleic acid and gamma-linolenic acid (GLA).[1]

Its main commercial use is as an oral dietary supplement, and it is also used in some skin products.[1] It has been examined in trials for atopic eczema, breast pain, menopausal symptoms and other conditions. A Cochrane review reported in reference sources found no effect on eczema, and the US National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NCCIH) is cited as finding the evidence insufficient to support use for any medical condition.[1][2]

paras: Indigenous peoples of North America used the plant as food and traditional medicine, and it reached Europe in the early 17th century as an ornamental garden plant.[1] Its modern use centres on the oil from its seeds as a supplement.[1]

EPO is promoted for skin health because of its GLA content, and it has been tested mainly in eczema rather than in cosmetic outcomes such as wrinkles or complexion. A systematic review of atopic eczema treatments assessed evening primrose oil among them.[4] No cosmetic-specific trials were identified in the sources.

Complementary-medicine reviews have assessed EPO for menopausal vasomotor symptoms, and the North American Menopause Society position statement addressed such treatments.[5][2] It has also been used or reviewed for breast pain, diabetic neuropathy, premenstrual symptoms and inflammatory bowel disease, with the Mayo Clinic cited as finding no good evidence for eczema, diabetic neuropathy or premenstrual syndrome.[1][6][7]

Reference sources describe EPO as likely safe at recommended amounts. Oral use may cause headache or nausea, and it may increase bleeding risk, which is relevant to people with bleeding disorders or those taking drugs that affect bleeding.[1] The Mayo Clinic is cited as advising caution for people with seizure disorders or mania and in pregnancy and breastfeeding.[1]

Reviews of herb-drug interactions and of complementary medicine use in cancer patients have discussed evening primrose among herbal products with potential interaction concerns, and laboratory work has tested herbal components for effects on cytochrome P450 enzymes.[8][9][10]

GLA, an omega-6 fatty acid, is a precursor of prostaglandin-type signalling molecules, which is the basis on which proponents suggest anti-inflammatory and skin-barrier effects. Studies comparing polyunsaturated fatty acid supplements have also reported effects of other fatty acids on immune cell function, for example fish oil and eicosapentaenoic acid.[11][12]

Trial registrations include EPO for breast-feeding pain (n=80),[13] induction of labour,[14] second-trimester missed miscarriage,[15][16] a vitamin E and EPO comparison for cyclical breast pain (n=82),[17] menopausal symptoms compared with lavender,[18] and a Phase 4 study of the prescription GLA product Epogam in atopic dermatitis (n=23).[3] A systematic review of eczema treatments and reviews of complementary treatments in menopause and inflammatory bowel disease have summarised randomised evidence.[4][5][7] Reference sources report that a Cochrane review found no benefit for eczema.[1] No clinical studies of EPO for facial skin appearance specifically were found.

timeline.event: Evening primrose reaches Europe as an ornamental plant.[1]
A Health Technology Assessment systematic review evaluates treatments for atopic eczema including EPO.[4]
A review of complementary therapies for menopausal symptoms is published.[5]
